evidence_quotes.quote: We examine the connection between incorporation status and access to centralized infrastructure, using negative binomial regression. A novel dataset informs this analysis, comprised of 31,383 Census block groups located in nine states representing over 25% of the national population.
Negative binomial models assess how incorporation status shapes access to centralized infrastructure.

Where unincorporated communities begin, sewer lines tend to wane. Island and Fringe communities might be especially prone to being underserved by sewer infrastructure due to municipal underbounding, extraterritorial jurisdiction, and state laws that restrict new incorporations in proximity to existing municipalities.

Negative binomial regression models are used to examine the relationship between infrastructure coverage, jurisdiction, and poverty. Our dependent variable is land area not served by centralized infrastructure, over the total block group area.
Our unit of analysis is the Census block group, since these are the smallest geographic areas for which the Census Bureau provides sample data.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines community-level access to centralized drinking water (community water systems, CWS) and wastewater/sewer infrastructure (publicly-owned treatment works, POTW) across residential settlements.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Plain wording: directly examines local legal jurisdiction and governance status (municipal incorporation vs. unincorporated county governance, annexation rules, and municipal extraterritorial planning jurisdiction). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: municipal incorporation status and legal municipal boundaries/extraterritorial jurisdiction (operationalized as Incorporated vs. Unincorporated Island, Fringe within the 1-mile municipal extraterritorial jurisdiction zone, and Outlying areas) constitute a legal-institutional and regulatory boundary structure directly governing utility service territories, annexation-linked service extensions, and community exclusion from municipal water and sewer systems rather than generic project delivery, behavioural promotion, or unanalysed macro-governance background. (While specific state/county annexation statutes are absorbed into random effects and discussed qualitatively, jurisdictional incorporation/boundary status itself is directly modeled as the primary exposure.)
criterion_notes.c3: Quantitative empirical study assembling a spatial dataset of 31,383 Census block groups across nine U.S. states and estimating multilevel negative binomial generalized linear models with county and state random effects.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports centralized sewer (POTW) and centralized drinking water (CWS) service coverage gaps, measured as the proportion/percentage of community land area within each Census block group unserved by centralized sewer or drinking water infrastructure (with Incidence Rate Ratios).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (31,383 Census block groups containing community land surpassing 250 parcels per square mile across nine U.S. states), exposure (municipal incorporation status: incorporated vs. unincorporated Island, Fringe, and Outlying, interacted with high poverty), outcome (proportion of block group community land area unserved by centralized sewer and centralized drinking water), and study design (cross-sectional spatial econometric analysis using multilevel negative binomial regression) are all clearly specified.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

study_design: Cross-sectional observational spatial econometric study using multilevel negative binomial generalized linear models with county and state random effects
population_and_sample: 31,383 Census block groups (unit of analysis) containing community land (settlements surpassing 250 parcels per square mile) across nine U.S. states (Connecticut, Florida, Kentucky, Mississippi, New Jersey, North Carolina, Rhode Island, Texas, and West Virginia), representing over 25% of the U.S. national population and over 10 million residents in unincorporated communities.
exposure: Municipal incorporation and jurisdictional boundary status at the Census block group level (incorporated vs. unincorporated, disaggregated into Island [at least one-third of perimeter within 480 m of municipal boundary], Fringe [within 1.6 km / 1 mile approximating municipal extraterritorial jurisdiction], and Outlying [>1.6 km from city limits]), and interaction with high poverty (20% or more of households below the Federal poverty line).
outcome: Proportion (and percentage) of community land area within a Census block group not served (unserved) by centralized wastewater/sewer infrastructure (POTW) and centralized drinking water infrastructure (CWS), estimated via Incidence Rate Ratios (IRRs).
rationale: This empirical quantitative study satisfies all inclusion criteria (c1-c6). It analyzes 31,383 U.S. Census block groups across nine states using multilevel negative binomial regression to test how legal-jurisdictional incorporation status and municipal boundary proximity/extraterritorial jurisdiction (Incorporated vs. Unincorporated Island, Fringe, and Outlying communities) govern exclusion from centralized drinking water and wastewater (sewer) service areas. It qualifies under both the plain wording and the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2 because municipal incorporation boundaries, underbounding, and extraterritorial jurisdiction are legal-institutional regulatory structures that directly govern utility service territories and community access to municipal water and sewer systems.
